sentences.text: Today, I want to teach you a lesson about stress.

Not the kind of stress you get when you've got to pay your taxes or your partner's upset with you, but stress in language, because many of you hear all the words, but don't understand what someone's actually saying.
Right, E?
Yeah, you said it.
You understand every word they say, but not what they mean together.
That's because language isn't just words.
We have intonation, and stress is one of those where we try to tell you what's important.
Okay?
So, I'm going to go to the board and I'm going to teach you today how we can use stress to communicate better when we speak, but also to understand when someone's speaking to us.
Ready?
Let's go to the board.
We're going to work on "spotlight".
I'm going to teach you a spotlight method to work with stress, and that's what this is here.
A spotlight is used when you want to show something very specific.
As you can see, I want you to just see Mr. E, so the spotlight comes down on Mr. E. It brings my attention to where I want you to go.
Okay?
So, let's give an example, alright?

Tony said it, but it wasn't me.

Why is this person angry?
Why is this person angry?
Why is this person...
Why?
The message was switched, because same words don't mean the same message.
When I stressed "I", for instance, right?
Stress tells you what is important.
When I say I didn't say she stole the money, I'm telling you my involvement, me, I didn't have anything to do with it, so me as the speaker, that's important, right?
